findings.lesson_title: Minerals: Properties and Identification
findings.claim: A measure of a mineral's resistance to scratching, expressed on a 1–10 scale devised by Friedrich Mohs in 1812.
findings.issue: The date 1812 is correct for when Mohs published the scale. No factual error; claim is accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Unconformities and Reading 3D Structures
findings.claim: near-vertical Silurian greywacke beds (around 435 million years old) are unconformably overlain by gently dipping Devonian red sandstone (around 370 million years old). The nearly 65-million-year gap in the record convinced James Hutton in 1788
findings.issue: The Silurian greywackes at Siccar Point are approximately 425–430 Ma (Llandovery–Wenlock), not 435 Ma. The Devonian sandstone is Old Red Sandstone, approximately 370–382 Ma. The time gap is approximately 45–65 million years depending on which sub-ages are used. '435 million years old' is slightly too old for the Silurian greywackes at this specific locality; the figure 425 Ma is more commonly cited. Minor rounding issue.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'around 435 million years old' to 'around 425–430 million years old' for the Silurian greywackes.

findings.lesson_title: Stratigraphic Principles and Relative Dating
findings.claim: Hutton first recognised the significance of unconformities at Siccar Point in Scotland in 1788, where near-vertical Silurian greywackes are overlain by gently dipping Devonian sandstones — a gap of tens of millions of years
findings.issue: Accurate overall, but consistent with the same minor age issue in Lesson 3 of structures unit. 'Tens of millions of years' is correct. No new severity issue here; consistent phrasing.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed in this lesson; the phrasing 'tens of millions of years' is accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
findings.claim: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the hypothesis of continental drift.
findings.issue: Accurate. Wegener first presented the idea in a 1912 lecture and paper. No error.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
findings.claim: identical fossils of the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus were found in both South America and southern Africa
findings.issue: Mesosaurus is correctly described as an aquatic reptile found in both South America and Africa. It is often described as freshwater or aquatic. Accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
findings.claim: Vine, Matthews, and separately Morley in 1963. They showed that the ocean floor displays parallel stripes of alternately normally and reversely magnetised basalt
findings.issue: Accurate. The Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis was published in 1963. Morley's paper was rejected first; Vine and Matthews published in September 1963. The attribution is correct.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
findings.claim: Tuzo Wilson added the concept of transform faults (1965)
findings.issue: Accurate. Wilson's 1965 paper 'A New Class of Faults and their Bearing on Continental Drift' introduced transform faults. Correct year and attribution.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
findings.claim: The oldest known rocks on Earth (the Acasta Gneiss of Canada) are around 4 billion years old
findings.issue: Slightly imprecise but acceptable at GCSE level. The Acasta Gneiss is dated to approximately 4.03 billion years old (4,028 Ma), so 'around 4 billion years old' is a reasonable approximation. No significant error.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed; 'around 4 billion years old' is an acceptable GCSE-level approximation of 4.03 Ga.

findings.lesson_title: Plate Boundaries and Their Products
findings.claim: The San Andreas Fault in California is the most studied example. Here the Pacific Plate slides north-west relative to the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year.
findings.issue: The movement rate of 5–6 cm per year is at the upper end of published estimates; most authoritative sources give 20–35 mm/year (2–3.5 cm/year) for the total slip rate along the entire fault, though some segments exceed 5 cm/year. The figure 5–6 cm/yr is defensible but slightly high as an overall average.
findings.suggested_fix: Consider changing to 'roughly 2–5 cm per year' to better reflect the full range of published slip rates along different segments of the fault.

findings.lesson_title: Plate Boundaries and Their Products
findings.claim: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific reaches over 11,000 m depth.
findings.issue: Accurate. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench reaches approximately 10,984 m, so 'over 11,000 m' is very slightly imprecise — the actual maximum is just under 11,000 m. However, the difference is within measurement uncertainty and commonly cited as ~11,000 m.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor: consider changing to 'approximately 11,000 m depth' or 'nearly 11,000 m'. The current phrasing 'over 11,000 m' is technically incorrect by a few metres.

findings.lesson_title: Plate Boundaries and Their Products
findings.claim: the Indian part of the Indo-Australian Plate has been colliding with the Eurasian Plate for roughly 50 million years
findings.issue: Accurate. India-Eurasia collision began approximately 50–55 Ma. Correct at GCSE level.

findings.lesson_title: Zone Fossils and Correlation
findings.claim: Graptolites were colonial animals that lived in the Palaeozoic era, predominantly from the Cambrian to the end of the Silurian (approximately 520 to 420 million years ago).
findings.issue: Graptolites did not go extinct at the end of the Silurian. They survived into the Devonian (final extinction approximately 370–376 Ma). The planktonic graptolites that are most important as zone fossils do largely disappear by the end of the Silurian/early Devonian, but the statement 'to the end of the Silurian' is an oversimplification that could mislead students. The BGS states graptolites lived from Cambrian to Late Devonian.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'predominantly from the Cambrian to the end of the Silurian (approximately 520 to 420 million years ago)' to 'predominantly from the Cambrian to the end of the Silurian as zone fossils (approximately 520 to 420 million years ago), with the group finally going extinct in the late Devonian'.

findings.lesson_title: Absolute Dating and Radioactive Decay
findings.claim: uranium-238 decays to lead-206 (half-life approximately 4.47 billion years)
findings.issue: Accurate. The half-life of U-238 is 4.468 billion years, commonly rounded to 4.47 Ga. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Absolute Dating and Radioactive Decay
findings.claim: potassium-40 decays to argon-40 (half-life approximately 1.25 billion years)
findings.issue: Accurate. The half-life of K-40 is 1.248 billion years, rounded to 1.25 Ga. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Absolute Dating and Radioactive Decay
findings.claim: carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 (half-life 5,730 years)
findings.issue: Accurate. The half-life of C-14 is 5,730 ± 40 years. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: In 1650, Archbishop James Ussher of Armagh calculated from biblical genealogies that the Earth was created in 4004 BC
findings.issue: Accurate. Ussher's Annales veteris testamenti was published in 1650. His calculation gave creation as 4004 BC. Correct title and year.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: James Hutton (1726–1797), a Scottish geologist
findings.issue: Accurate. Hutton's dates are confirmed as 1726–1797. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: Lord Kelvin (William Thomson, 1824–1907) was the dominant physicist of the nineteenth century. In 1862, he calculated how long it would have taken a molten Earth to cool to its present temperature gradient
findings.issue: Accurate. Kelvin published his cooling calculation in 1862. His dates (1824–1907) are correct.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: radioactivity, which was not discovered until 1896 by Henri Becquerel
findings.issue: Accurate. Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: John Joly (1857–1933), an Irish physicist…In 1899, he published an estimate of approximately 90 million years.
findings.issue: Accurate. Joly's dates (1857–1933) are confirmed. His 1899 ocean salinity estimate of ~90 million years is confirmed. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Deep Time and the Age of the Earth
findings.claim: Arthur Holmes (1890–1965) was the scientist who finally put a reliable number on the age of the Earth…In 1913, he published the first geological time scale with ages in millions of years derived from isotope measurements, giving the oldest rocks an age of about 1,600 million years.
findings.issue: Accurate. Holmes published The Age of the Earth in 1913, estimating the oldest rocks at about 1,600 million years. His dates (1890–1965) are confirmed. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: The oldest confirmed evidence of life on Earth comes from stromatolites…found in rocks approximately 3,500 million years old (3,500 Ma).
findings.issue: Accurate at GCSE level. The oldest widely accepted stromatolite evidence is ~3,500 Ma (Apex Chert, Pilbara, Australia). Correct.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: The Cambrian Explosion…is spectacularly documented in the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, Canada (approximately 508 Ma).
findings.issue: Accurate. The Burgess Shale dates to approximately 508 Ma (Middle Cambrian). Correct location and age.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: Archaeopteryx, discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany in 1861, is one of the most famous fossils in science. Aged at approximately 150 Ma (Jurassic)
findings.issue: Accurate. Archaeopteryx was first described in 1861 from the Solnhofen Limestone, Germany, and dates to ~150 Ma (Late Jurassic). Correct.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) is a partial skeleton discovered in Ethiopia in 1974, aged approximately 3.2 million years old.
findings.issue: Accurate. Lucy was discovered by Donald Johanson in Ethiopia on 24 November 1974, dated to 3.2 Ma. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: The most severe was the end-Permian extinction (approximately 252 Ma), which wiped out an estimated 90 to 96% of marine species.
findings.issue: The range 90–96% is the commonly cited range for end-Permian marine species loss and is well supported in the literature. Technically, some analyses give slightly lower figures (81–94%). The text's claim is at the upper end but within accepted scientific range. Acceptable.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed; 90–96% is widely cited and defensible.

findings.lesson_title: The Origin and Development of Life
findings.claim: the Chicxulub crater in Mexico (approximately 180 km in diameter)
findings.issue: The Chicxulub crater is approximately 200 km (120 miles) in diameter, not 180 km. Multiple authoritative sources including Wikipedia, Britannica, and USGS consistently give ~200 km. The lesson understates the diameter by 20 km.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'approximately 180 km in diameter' to 'approximately 200 km in diameter'.

findings.lesson_title: Icehouse and Greenhouse Earth
findings.claim: Cretaceous period (roughly 145–66 million years ago)…global temperatures were 6–10°C warmer than today and sea levels were 100–200 m higher than at present
findings.issue: The Cretaceous date range (145–66 Ma) is correct. The temperature and sea level figures are within broadly accepted ranges for Cretaceous greenhouse conditions. Acceptable.

findings.lesson_title: Planetary Geology: Earth and Its Neighbours
findings.claim: Olympus Mons, standing about 22 km above the surrounding plains and measuring about 600 km across at its base.
findings.issue: The height is slightly overstated. Olympus Mons stands 21.1–21.3 km tall, not 22 km. The diameter of ~600 km is correct. The lesson's key fact box later says 'about 22 km tall' but the accurate figure is 21.1–21.3 km. Minor rounding, but consistently stated as 22 km when the correct value is ~21 km.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'about 22 km' to 'about 21 km' (or 'approximately 21–22 km') to match the actual height of 21.1–21.3 km.

findings.lesson_title: Planetary Geology: Earth and Its Neighbours
findings.claim: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 22 km tall — nearly three times the height of Mauna Kea from its ocean base.
findings.issue: Mauna Kea is approximately 10.2 km from its ocean base. Olympus Mons at ~21 km is approximately twice the height of Mauna Kea from its base, not 'nearly three times'. The ratio is approximately 2:1, not 3:1.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 'nearly three times the height of Mauna Kea from its ocean base' to 'approximately twice the height of Mauna Kea from its ocean base'.

findings.lesson_title: Impacts, Craters and Planetary History
findings.claim: Jezero Crater, which is approximately 49 km wide.
findings.issue: Multiple authoritative sources give the diameter of Jezero Crater as approximately 45–49 km. Wikipedia gives 45.0 km; other NASA sources say 49 km. There is some variation between sources. The lesson's figure of 49 km is at the upper end of published estimates but not clearly wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Consider changing to 'approximately 45–49 km wide' to acknowledge the variation in published estimates, or use 'approximately 45 km wide' which is the most commonly cited figure.

findings.lesson_title: Impacts, Craters and Planetary History
findings.claim: the Sudbury Basin in Canada, for example, is a 1.85-billion-year-old impact structure that hosts one of the world's largest nickel-copper ore deposits
findings.issue: Accurate. The Sudbury Basin is dated to approximately 1.85 billion years ago and is indeed one of the world's largest nickel-copper deposits. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Impacts, Craters and Planetary History
findings.claim: The impactor was roughly 10 km in diameter and released energy equivalent to billions of nuclear weapons.
findings.issue: The ~10 km impactor diameter is the standard figure for the Chicxulub impactor. Accurate.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Hazards: Earthquakes, Eruptions, Landslides and Tsunamis
findings.claim: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0) off Japan
findings.issue: The magnitude of the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake is given variously as 9.0–9.1 Mw; 9.0 is the most widely cited initial figure and was the official USGS magnitude. Acceptable.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed; 9.0 is the standard published magnitude.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Hazards: Earthquakes, Eruptions, Landslides and Tsunamis
findings.claim: The 1980 Mount St Helens eruption was VEI 5; the 1991 Pinatubo eruption was VEI 6.
findings.issue: Accurate. Mount St Helens 1980 is VEI 5 and Pinatubo 1991 is VEI 6. Both confirmed by USGS. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Earth Hazards: Earthquakes, Eruptions, Landslides and Tsunamis
findings.claim: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra, generated waves exceeding 30 metres in parts of Aceh province, Indonesia, killing over 230,000 people across 14 countries.
findings.issue: Accurate. Magnitude 9.1 (some sources say 9.2–9.3 but 9.1 is widely cited). Wave heights in Aceh exceeded 30 m at some locations. Death toll ~230,000. 14 countries affected. All figures confirmed.

findings.lesson_title: Predicting and Mitigating Earth Hazards
findings.claim: After a two-month period of intense monitoring, scientists detected a growing bulge on Mount St Helens' north flank…When the eruption occurred on 18 May 1980, the lateral blast killed 57 people
findings.issue: Accurate. The eruption killed 57 people on 18 May 1980. The two-month precursor monitoring is consistent with known chronology. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Predicting and Mitigating Earth Hazards
findings.claim: The 2010 Haiti earthquake (magnitude 7.0) killed around 230,000 people
findings.issue: Magnitude 7.0 is confirmed. The death toll of around 230,000 is at the higher end of estimates; the Haitian government reported up to 316,000, while independent estimates range from 100,000–160,000. The figure 230,000 is a commonly cited government-reported figure but is disputed. At GCSE level this is acceptable.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed at GCSE level; 230,000 is a commonly cited figure even though total death toll estimates vary.

findings.lesson_title: Predicting and Mitigating Earth Hazards
findings.claim: The 2009 L'Aquila earthquake in Italy killed 309 people
findings.issue: Most sources give 308 deaths; some give 309. The discrepancy of one person is trivial. No meaningful error.
findings.suggested_fix: No change needed; the difference between 308 and 309 is immaterial at GCSE level.

findings.lesson_title: Oil, Gas and Energy Resources
findings.claim: the 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout in the Gulf of Mexico released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil
findings.issue: Accurate. The US government estimated total discharge at 4.9 million barrels. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Geology and Civil Engineering
findings.claim: The 1928 St Francis Dam failure in California killed over 400 people; investigation revealed the dam had been built on a fault zone and across a contact between two incompatible rock types that differentially weakened under reservoir loading.
findings.issue: The death toll was approximately 425 people, so 'over 400' is accurate. However, the geological cause description is incomplete/slightly misleading. The primary failure causes were: (1) a thrust fault on the western abutment; (2) swelling and slaking of Sespe conglomerate on the western side; (3) a landslide on the eastern abutment in weak schist. The lesson correctly identifies the fault zone but phrases 'two incompatible rock types' which, while broadly accurate (schist on east, conglomerate on west), oversimplifies the multi-cause failure. The stated cause is not wrong but is incomplete.
findings.suggested_fix: The lesson's description is broadly acceptable for GCSE. If desired, clarify: 'investigation revealed the dam had been built on a thrust fault zone, with weak conglomerate on one abutment that swelled when saturated, and unstable schist on the other.' The death toll 'over 400' is correct.

findings.lesson_title: Metamorphic Rocks: Heat, Pressure and Texture
findings.claim: Classic Welsh slate (quarried at Blaenau Ffestiniog) is a textbook example.
findings.issue: Accurate. Blaenau Ffestiniog in North Wales is a major slate quarrying centre. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Folding and Tectonic Stress
findings.claim: the Caledonian mountain-building event — caused by the collision of ancient plates during the Silurian and Devonian periods — produced the folded and faulted rocks now exposed in the Scottish Highlands and parts of Wales.
findings.issue: Accurate. The Caledonian orogeny (spanning approximately 490–390 Ma, peaking in Silurian–Early Devonian) produced the deformed rocks of the Scottish Highlands and parts of Wales. Correct.

findings.lesson_title: Faults and Fault Displacement
findings.claim: The Moine Thrust in north-west Scotland is a famous example, where ancient Precambrian rocks were thrust horizontally over younger Cambrian strata during the Caledonian orogeny.
findings.issue: Accurate. The Moine Thrust Belt thrust Precambrian Moine metasediments and Lewisian gneisses over Cambro-Ordovician sediments during the Caledonian orogeny (Scandian phase, ~430–400 Ma). Correct.
